title: Hash Function
body:
The function that turns a key into a table index: $h(\text{key}) \rightarrow [0, m)$ for a
table of $m$ slots. It is the engine of [[Hashing]], and the quality of the whole [[Hash Map]]
is the quality of this one function.

Three requirements:

1. **Deterministic.** The same key must always give the same index, or you can never find
   what you stored.
2. **Fast.** It runs on every single operation. A hash that costs $O(n)$ has thrown away the
   reason for hashing.
3. **Uniform.** It should spread keys evenly across the table. Clumping means collisions,
   and enough collisions turn $O(1)$ lookup into an $O(n)$ scan.

## The usual shape

Convert the key to an integer, then squeeze it into range with modulo:

```java
int hash(String key, int m) {
    int h = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < key.length(); i++)
        h = 31 * h + key.charAt(i);      // 31: odd prime, and 31*h compiles to a shift-subtract
    return Math.abs(h) % m;
}
```

The multiply-and-add makes the result depend on character *position*, so `"stop"` and
`"pots"` hash differently. A hash that just sums the characters does not, and that is a
classic way to get a table full of collisions.

## Table size

Take $m$ to be a [[Prime Number]]. Modulo by a power of two keeps only the low bits of the
hash and throws away the rest, so any pattern in those bits (keys that are all multiples of
4, say) collides immediately. A prime modulus mixes the whole value in. Libraries that do
use power-of-two tables compensate by scrambling the bits first, which amounts to the same
defence.

## What this is not

This is not a cryptographic hash. SHA-256 and friends are also key-to-number functions, but
they are designed so that the input cannot be recovered and collisions cannot be constructed
on purpose, and they are far too slow to sit in a table lookup. Same word, different job:
see [[CRYPTOGRAPHY]].
